pos: v. (to devise, to contrive; in the Authorized Version almost always of plotting, not of picturing)
etymology: Latin imaginari, to form an image in the mind. The Hebrew hagah and chashab behind the KJV usage mean to mutter over a thing and to reckon or contrive it — the mind at work on a plan.
biblical_def: Modern English uses imagine for harmless fancy. The Authorized Version almost never does. To imagine in Scripture is to devise, and what is devised is nearly always mischief. “Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?” (Psa 2:1) — the nations are not daydreaming, they are conspiring, as the next verse shows: “The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD, and against his anointed” (Psa 2:2). Job's friends imagine devices wrongfully against him (Job 21:27), and the psalmist's enemies “imagine deceits all the day long” (Psa 38:12). The reason the word carries this weight is stated at the flood: “every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually” (Gen 6:5). The faculty is not neutral. Fallen men do not merely have bad thoughts; the inventive power itself has been turned, so that Proverbs can speak of “An heart that deviseth wicked imaginations” (Pro 6:18). The New Testament answer is not to empty the mind but to conquer it: “Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ” (2Co 10:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to imagine as to form a notion or idea in the mind; to fancy; and secondly, to contrive in purpose, to scheme, to devise — which is the Scripture sense.
webster_full: IMAGINE, v.t. [L. imaginor, from imago, an image.] To form a notion or idea in the mind; to fancy.
In the night imagining some fear, how easy is a bush supposed a bear.
2. To form ideas or representations in the mind, by modifying and combining our conceptions.
3. To contrive in purpose; to scheme; to devise. How long will ye imagine mischief against a man? Ps. lxii.
scriptures: Psa 2:1
Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?
Gen 6:5
And GOD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.
They also that seek after my life lay snares for me: and they that seek my hurt speak mischievous things, and imagine deceits all the day long.
Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ;
corruption_summary: Imagination is now treated as an innocent faculty and even as the seat of hope, while Genesis 6:5 locates original corruption precisely there.
corruption_paragraphs: It is a settled assumption of our age that the imagination is where a man is at his best — the source of creativity, vision, and the capacity to conceive a better world. Scripture makes it the very place the fall is inspected. What God saw before the flood was not chiefly deeds but every imagination of the thoughts of his heart, and the verdict was that it was only evil continually. That is not an argument against the arts, and the Bible itself is full of images, parables and songs made by men under the Spirit. It is an argument against the confidence that whatever the heart conceives is worth following. When a man is told to trust his vision, he is being told to trust the one faculty Genesis names as thoroughly bent, and the counsel is offered with no examination at all of whether the vision is true.

The corollary corruption is in the doctrine of prayer and of guidance, where imagining has quietly become a means of grace. A man is taught to picture the outcome he desires, to hold the image, and to speak of the image as faith; the practice comes into the churches from the prosperity teachers and stays because it feels devout. But faith in Scripture rests on a word God has actually spoken, not on a picture a man has formed, and 1 Corinthians 2:9 says flatly that the things God has prepared have not entered into the heart of man — the imagination cannot reach them, which is why they must be revealed. Paul's remedy in 2 Corinthians 10:5 is military language and it is the right register: imaginations are cast down, high things are pulled from their height, thoughts are taken captive and marched into the obedience of Christ. The Christian does not empty his mind; he conquers it, and the weapon is the word.
roots_summary: Hebrew hagah (H1897), to mutter or meditate, hence to plot; chashab (H2803), to reckon or devise; yetser (H3336), the thing framed, the imagination of Genesis 6:5; Greek logismos (G3053), a reasoning.
roots_lines: Hebrew hagah (H1897) — to mutter, to meditate, to plot; the heathen imagine a vain thing, and the righteous man meditates in the law; Psalm 2:1, Psalm 1:2.
Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to reckon, to devise, to contrive; used of imagining deceits and of God reckoning righteousness to Abraham; Psalm 38:12, Genesis 15:6.
Hebrew yetser (H3336) — the thing formed or framed, the imagination; from yatsar, to fashion as a potter; Genesis 6:5, Genesis 8:21.
Greek logismos (G3053) — a reasoning, a computation; rendered imaginations where they are cast down; 2 Corinthians 10:5.
Greek dialogismos (G1261) — a reasoning through, a disputing thought; they became vain in their imaginations; Romans 1:21.
usage: “The people imagine a vain thing” — not daydreaming, conspiring.
“Every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually” — the faculty itself inspected.
“Bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ” — conquest, not emptiness.

pos: v. (to purpose, to mean to do; the settled aim of the will before the act)
etymology: Latin intendere, to stretch toward, from in-, toward, and tendere, to stretch — the mind stretched out after an object. The Greek mello means to be about to do a thing.
biblical_def: Intention is what a man is stretching toward, and Scripture treats it as a real thing that can be examined and judged. When the western tribes built their altar, the rest of Israel armed for war until the purpose was explained, and then “the children of Israel blessed God, and did not intend to go up against them in battle” (Jos 22:33) — a war was stopped by discovering an intention. Oded warns Israel that they are about to compound a national sin: “ye intend to add more to our sins and to our trespass” (2Ch 28:13). The Sanhedrin accuses the apostles of an intention: “ye have filled Jerusalem with your doctrine, and intend to bring this man's blood upon us” (Act 5:28), and Gamaliel answers with the soberest counsel in the chapter: “take heed to yourselves what ye intend to do as touching these men” (Act 5:35). The Lord Jesus makes intention the point of a parable about counting: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?” (Luk 14:28). And James sets the boundary that keeps intending from becoming boasting: “For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that” (Jas 4:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to intend as to stretch or extend, and hence to design, to purpose, to fix the mind upon as a thing to be done or accomplished.
webster_full: INTEND, v.t. [L. intendo; in and tendo, to tend, to stretch.] To stretch; to extend.
2. To design; to purpose; to fix the mind on as a thing to be done or accomplished.
Intending to build a tower. Luke xiv.
3. To regard; to fix the mind on; to attend.
scriptures: And the thing pleased the children of Israel; and the children of Israel blessed God, and did not intend to go up against them in battle, to destroy the land wherein the children of Reuben and Gad dwelt.
Act 5:35
And said unto them, Ye men of Israel, take heed to yourselves what ye intend to do as touching these men.
For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?
Jas 4:15
For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.
corruption_summary: Good intentions have become a defence against the judgment of actions, though Scripture judges the intention and the act together and never lets one excuse the other.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors run about intention and both are common. The first says that intention is everything: a man who meant well cannot be blamed for what he did, and to raise the outcome is to be unkind. Scripture will not have it. Uzzah meant to steady the ark and died; the law provided a city of refuge for the man who killed unawares, which is precisely an acknowledgment that a death has happened even where the intent was absent. Meaning well does not undo a wrong, though it changes how the wrong is dealt with. The second error says intention is nothing, and only results are moral. Scripture will not have that either: the Lord names the look as adultery and the hatred as murder, because the will has already stretched toward the thing. A man is answerable for what he aimed at and for what he did.

The pastoral use of the word is at Luke 14:28. The Lord makes intending to build a tower the picture of intending to follow Him, and the whole force of the parable is that an intention untested by counting is worthless. Our own religious culture is full of intention treated as achievement — the resolution announced, the commitment made publicly, the plan for discipleship laid out in detail — and it is precisely what the Lord tells men not to do until they have sat down and reckoned. Gamaliel's warning is the other side of it. Take heed to yourselves what ye intend to do: an intention is a thing a man can be warned off before he has moved a hand, because God sees it already. James supplies the only safe way to hold any intention at all, which is under the will of God — not as a pious tag on the end of a plan, but as an honest acknowledgment that the man who intends does not own tomorrow.
roots_summary: Greek mello (G3195), to be about to do; boulomai (G1014), to will or purpose deliberately; Hebrew zamam (H2161), to purpose or devise.
roots_lines: Greek mello (G3195) — to be about to, to intend; what the council intended to do, and what a man intends to build; Acts 5:35, Luke 14:28.
Greek boulomai (G1014) — to will, to purpose after deliberation; used of God's determinate purpose and of a man's settled intent; Hebrews 6:17, James 4:4.
Hebrew zamam (H2161) — to purpose, to devise; the LORD hath done that which he had devised; Lamentations 2:17.
Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to reckon, to intend; ye thought evil against me, but God meant it unto good; Genesis 50:20.
Greek prothesis (G4286) — a setting forth, a purpose; the purpose of God according to election; Romans 9:11, Ephesians 1:11.
usage: “Did not intend to go up against them in battle” — a war stopped by an intention discovered.
“Take heed to yourselves what ye intend to do” — a man warned off before his hand moves.
“Intending to build a tower” — the intention that must be counted before it is announced.

pos: v. (to come to oneself; to recollect and consider, as the first motion of repentance)
etymology: Old English bethencan, to think about, to call to mind. The Hebrew at 2 Chronicles 6 is shub el leb, to bring back to the heart — the exile turning his thoughts homeward before he turns his feet.
biblical_def: The word occurs once in the Authorized Version, in Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple, and it names the first motion of a returning sinner. Solomon foresees the captivity and prays: “Yet if they bethink themselves in the land whither they are carried captive, and turn and pray unto thee in the land of their captivity, saying, We have sinned, we have done amiss, and have dealt wickedly” (2Ch 6:37). The order of the verbs is the doctrine. First they bethink themselves — the mind comes back to the heart, the man stops and considers where he is and how he came there. Then they turn. Then they pray. Then they confess in the plainest words a man can use: we have sinned, we have done amiss, and have dealt wickedly. The Lord Jesus paints the same sequence in the far country, where the prodigal “came to himself” before he ever said I will arise (Luk 15:17). Repentance begins in the understanding, but it does not stay there; a bethinking that never turns is only regret. The mercy of the passage is that Solomon prays for it in advance, and that God grants such thinking to men already under judgment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to bethink as to call to mind; to recall or bring to recollection, reflection or consideration; generally used with a reciprocal pronoun.
webster_full: BETHINK, v.t. To call to mind; to recall or bring to recollection, reflection or consideration; generally followed by a reciprocal pronoun.
I have bethought myself of a plan.
BETHINK, v.i. To have in recollection; to consider.
If they bethink themselves in the land whither they are carried captive. 2 Chron. vi.
scriptures: Yet if they bethink themselves in the land whither they are carried captive, and turn and pray unto thee in the land of their captivity, saying, We have sinned, we have done amiss, and have dealt wickedly;
And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father's have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!
Now consider this, ye that forget God, lest I tear you in pieces, and there be none to deliver.
Jer 3:22
Return, ye backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings. Behold, we come unto thee; for thou art the LORD our God.
corruption_summary: Repentance is widely presented as a change of feeling, when Scripture begins it in the understanding — a man bethinking himself — and completes it in the will.
corruption_paragraphs: Two truncated accounts of repentance circulate, and each keeps one part of 2 Chronicles 6:37 while dropping the rest. The first makes repentance a feeling: a man is sorry, and the sorrow is the whole transaction. Paul distinguishes godly sorrow, which worketh repentance, from the sorrow of the world, which worketh death, and the distinction is exactly that the one turns and the other only aches. The second makes repentance a decision: a moment recorded, a card signed, a hand raised, with no consideration behind it and no turning after it. Solomon's prayer has four movements and will not spare one — bethink, turn, pray, confess — and the confession he supplies is not a general acknowledgment of imperfection but three plain admissions in a row.

The place this bites hardest is the doctrine of assurance. A man who was told that his sorrow or his decision was the whole of repentance has nothing to examine himself by afterwards, so when the feeling cools he concludes either that he was never converted or that the matter is settled and needs no further attention. Neither conclusion is drawn from Scripture. Solomon's captives bethink themselves in the land whither they are carried — that is, in the middle of the consequences, with no altar, no temple, and no priest at hand — and God hears them there. The prodigal comes to himself among the swine. The comfort in both cases is that God gives the very thinking by which men return, and the warning in Psalm 50:22 is set beside it: consider this, ye that forget God. Forgetting is the disease; bethinking is the beginning of the cure, and it is a gift.
roots_summary: Hebrew shub (H7725), to turn back, the standard verb of repentance, joined at 2 Chronicles 6:37 with leb (H3820), the heart; Greek metanoia (G3341), a change of mind.
roots_lines: Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn, to return; the great prophetic call, and the second verb of Solomon's sequence; 2 Chronicles 6:37, Jeremiah 3:22.
Hebrew leb (H3820) — the heart, the seat of thought as well as affection; to bring a thing back to the heart is to consider it; Deuteronomy 4:39.
Hebrew chata (H2398) — to sin, to miss; the first word of the captives' confession, we have sinned; 2 Chronicles 6:37.
Greek metanoia (G3341) — a change of mind, repentance; the New Testament word that carries Solomon's whole sequence; Acts 11:18.
Greek erchomai eis heauton — to come to oneself; the phrase of the prodigal, the exact equivalent of bethinking; Luke 15:17.
usage: “If they bethink themselves in the land whither they are carried captive” — repentance beginning under the judgment.
“When he came to himself” — the same motion in the far country.
“Consider this, ye that forget God” — the warning that stands beside the mercy.

pos: v. (to scheme beforehand; in Daniel, to contrive devices against another)
etymology: English fore-, before, with cast, to throw or reckon — to cast up an account in advance. In Daniel 11 the sense is wholly hostile: to lay plans against a man.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, in the great prophecy of the kings of the north and south: “And he shall stir up his power and his courage against the king of the south with a great army; and the king of the south shall be stirred up to battle with a very great and mighty army; but he shall not stand: for they shall forecast devices against him” (Dan 11:25). The forecasting is not weather-watching but conspiracy; the king of the south falls not for want of soldiers but because men at his own table have cast up a plan against him. That is the point of the whole chapter, in which armies are raised and treaties made and none of it moves an inch outside what was written beforehand. Daniel is given the plans of men centuries in advance, which is the strongest possible statement of who actually forecasts. The LORD says it of Himself: “Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure” (Isa 46:10). Proverbs states the same truth in the compass of a household: “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to forecast as to foresee, to provide against, to scheme or plan before execution; and as a noun, foresight of consequences and provision against them.
webster_full: FORECAST, v.t. To foresee; to provide against.
2. To scheme; to plan before execution. They shall forecast devices against him. Dan. xi.
FORECAST, v.i. To form a scheme previously; to contrive beforehand.
FORECAST, n. Foresight of consequences, and provision against them; previous contrivance.
scriptures: And he shall stir up his power and his courage against the king of the south with a great army; and the king of the south shall be stirred up to battle with a very great and mighty army; but he shall not stand: for they shall forecast devices against him.
Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:
Pro 16:9
A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.
The counsel of the LORD standeth for ever, the thoughts of his heart to all generations.
corruption_summary: Prediction has become the chief authority of public life, and men who cannot tell what shall be on the morrow speak of the future in the tone Isaiah 46:10 reserves for God.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing wrong with foresight; Scripture commends the ant, the prudent man who foreseeth the evil, and the builder who counts his cost. What Daniel names is different. To forecast devices against him is to use foresight as a weapon — to model another man's weaknesses and lay the plan that exploits them. The chapter shows it working at the level of empires, but the same faculty runs a family or a congregation, and the mark of it is that the planning is done about a person rather than with him. A man who finds himself rehearsing how a conversation must be steered, what must be withheld, and which allies must be secured first, has crossed from prudence into forecasting devices, whatever the cause he thinks he serves.

The second corruption is a whole civilisation's and it lives in the tone. Projections are issued about markets, populations, climates and the fortunes of nations in language of settled certainty, and the men who issue them are seldom held to account when the years arrive and disprove them. The Christian answer is not contempt for measurement, which is a good gift, but the recovery of the distinction Isaiah draws. God alone declares the end from the beginning, because He alone has decreed it; every other forecast is an estimate made from inside the thing being estimated. That is why James tells believers to say if the Lord will, and why Proverbs sets the two clauses side by side without any embarrassment — the man devises his way, and it is the LORD who directs his steps. Both are true, and the second governs the first.
roots_summary: Hebrew chashab (H2803), to reckon or devise, with machashabah (H4284), a device or plan; set against the LORD's etsah (H6098), counsel that stands.
roots_lines: Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to reckon, to contrive; rendered forecast where devices are laid against the king; Daniel 11:25.
Hebrew machashabah (H4284) — a device, a plan, a thought; the devices of the heathen brought to nought; Psalm 33:10.
Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel, purpose; the counsel of the LORD that standeth for ever; Psalm 33:11, Isaiah 46:10.
Hebrew kun (H3559) — to establish, to direct; the LORD directeth the steps of the man who devised his way; Proverbs 16:9.
Greek proginosko (G4267) — to know beforehand; the foreknowledge that belongs to God and not to the forecaster; Romans 8:29.
usage: “They shall forecast devices against him” — foresight turned into a weapon.
“Declaring the end from the beginning” — the only forecasting that is certain.
“A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” — both true, and the second governs.

pos: v. (to counsel; to give one's judgment on a course of action)
etymology: Old French aviser, from Latin ad visum, according to what is seen — to give the judgment one's view supplies. The Hebrew yaats is the standard verb of counsel, from which comes Wonderful, Counsellor.
biblical_def: The word enters the histories at the hinge of the divided kingdom. Rehoboam “consulted with the old men, that stood before Solomon his father while he yet lived, and said, How do ye advise that I may answer this people?” (1Ki 12:6). He asked well and then refused the answer: “But he forsook the counsel of the old men, which they had given him, and consulted with the young men that were grown up with him” (1Ki 12:8), and ten tribes were torn away. Asking for advice is not the same as taking it, and a man who seeks counsel until he finds the counsel he wanted has not sought counsel at all. Proverbs is emphatic on both the necessity and the plurality: “Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established” (Pro 15:22); “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14). The histories also record the danger of a counsellor too much trusted — Ahithophel's advice “was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God” (2Sa 16:23) — and that same counsellor turned traitor. Advice is a gift of God through men, and it is never the oracle.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to advise as to give counsel to; to offer an opinion as worthy or expedient to be followed; and to advise with, to consult and deliberate together.
webster_full: ADVISE, v.t. [Fr. aviser; ad and visum.] To give counsel to; to offer an opinion, as worthy or expedient to be followed.
I advise thee to the contrary.
2. To give information; to communicate notice; to make acquainted with.
ADVISE, v.i. To deliberate, weigh well, or consider. Advise thyself of what word I shall bring again. 1 Chron. xxi.
scriptures: And king Rehoboam consulted with the old men, that stood before Solomon his father while he yet lived, and said, How do ye advise that I may answer this people?
But he forsook the counsel of the old men, which they had given him, and consulted with the young men that were grown up with him, and which stood before him:
Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.
Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
corruption_summary: Counsel is now sought as confirmation rather than as correction, which is precisely Rehoboam's method and produced precisely his result.
corruption_paragraphs: Rehoboam's failure is not that he neglected to ask. He asked twice, and the second asking was the sin. He had a decision already formed and went looking for men who would sign it — men grown up with him, who shared his assumptions and owed him their prospects. Everything about the method looks diligent from outside. The corruption is quiet, common, and it is the ordinary way advice is sought today: a man circulates his plan among those most likely to approve it, calls the approval counsel, and proceeds fortified. Proverbs prescribes a multitude of counsellors precisely because a multitude is harder to select for agreement, and the old men Rehoboam rejected had one qualification the young men lacked — they had stood before Solomon and had watched what heavy yokes cost.

The opposite error is Ahithophel's, and it is the error of the one who receives counsel too well. His advice was esteemed as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God, and that estimate was a snare to David's house long before the man betrayed it. A counsellor is a means, not a mouth of God; where a Christian assigns to a pastor, a mentor, or a gifted friend an authority that belongs only to Scripture, he has made an oracle of a man and will be wounded when the man proves to be one. The Reformed doctrine of the sufficiency of Scripture is not hostile to counsel — the same Bible commands it in the plainest terms — but it fixes counsel in its place: advice is weighed by the word, never above it, and the wisest counsellor in Israel hanged himself when his advice was not taken.
roots_summary: Hebrew yaats (H3289), to advise or counsel, with etsah (H6098), counsel, and yoets (H3289), a counsellor; Greek sumbouleuo (G4823), to counsel together.
roots_lines: Hebrew yaats (H3289) — to advise, to counsel; how do ye advise that I may answer this people; 1 Kings 12:6.
Hebrew etsah (H6098) — counsel, the thing advised; forsaken by Rehoboam and standing for ever in the LORD; 1 Kings 12:8, Psalm 33:11.
Hebrew yoets — a counsellor; the child born to us is called Wonderful, Counsellor; Isaiah 9:6.
Hebrew sod (H5475) — intimate counsel, a confidential circle; the secret of the LORD is with them that fear him; Psalm 25:14.
Greek sumbouleuo (G4823) — to counsel together, to take counsel with; used both of godly consultation and of the plot against Christ; Matthew 26:4.
usage: “How do ye advise that I may answer this people?” — the right question, asked by the wrong heart.
“He forsook the counsel of the old men” — asking twice until the answer agreed.
“In the multitude of counsellors there is safety” — a multitude is harder to select for agreement.

pos: v. and n. (to mark down, to set a mark upon; also a mark of distinction, as of note)
etymology: Latin nota, a mark, a sign, a written character. The verb runs two ways in Scripture: to write a thing down so that it stands for the time to come, and to mark a man out for the church's discipline.
biblical_def: Isaiah is commanded to make a record that will outlive him: “Now go, write it before them in a table, and note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come for ever and ever” (Isa 30:8). Habakkuk receives the same charge in different words: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2). Prophecy is committed to writing on purpose, so that a later generation can check what was said against what came — the whole doctrine of an inscripturated word is present in the command. The second use is the church's: “And if any man obey not our word by this epistle, note that man, and have no company with him, that he may be ashamed” (2Th 3:14). Here noting is the congregation marking a disobedient brother, and the stated aim is not his destruction but his shame unto repentance — the next verse forbids counting him an enemy and requires admonishing him as a brother. A third sense is honour: Andronicus and Junia are “of note among the apostles” (Rom 16:7). Scripture notes men down for warning and for honour, and it does both in writing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a note as a mark or token; a character or sign; a short writing or memorandum; and to note as to observe carefully, to mark, or to set down in writing.
webster_full: NOTE, n. [L. nota.] A mark or token; something by which a thing may be known; a visible sign.
2. A short writing; a memorandum; a minute.
3. Reputation; consequence; distinction; as men of note.
NOTE, v.t. To observe; to notice with particular care; to heed; to attend to. Note that man, and have no company with him. 2 Thess. iii.
scriptures: Isa 30:8
Now go, write it before them in a table, and note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come for ever and ever:
Hab 2:2
And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
And if any man obey not our word by this epistle, note that man, and have no company with him, that he may be ashamed.
Rom 16:7
Salute Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen, and my fellowprisoners, who are of note among the apostles, who also were in Christ before me.
corruption_summary: The apostolic command to note a disobedient man is now felt to be unloving, though Paul gives the aim in the same sentence — that he may be ashamed — and forbids treating him as an enemy in the next.
corruption_paragraphs: Church discipline has quietly fallen out of use in most congregations, and where it is mentioned it is defended or attacked in terms Paul never uses. The command at 2 Thessalonians 3:14 is short and unembarrassed: note that man, and have no company with him. Two things are worth marking. The first is that the ground is disobedience to apostolic teaching, not personality, not preference, and not a quarrel with the leadership; discipline that is used to protect a pastor's position rather than the church's obedience is the abuse, and the abuse does not abolish the ordinance. The second is that the aim is stated: that he may be ashamed. Shame is not here a wound inflicted for its own sake but the God-given pain by which a man who has grown comfortable in sin is made uncomfortable enough to return, and the very next verse guards it — count him not as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.

The other half of the word bears on how we hold the Scriptures themselves. Isaiah is told to note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come. The written form is not a lesser vehicle than the spoken one; it is given precisely so the word can be examined by generations that never heard the prophet's voice. That cuts against the notion, common wherever fresh revelation is claimed, that the living voice in the room outranks the settled text — the prophets themselves were sent to the book. It also puts a duty on the reader. A written word can be checked, and Habakkuk says it is made plain so that he may run that readeth it: plain enough to be understood, and public enough that no man needs an authorised interpreter standing between him and the page.
roots_summary: Hebrew chaqaq (H2710), to inscribe or engrave, rendered note at Isaiah 30:8; Greek semeioo (G4593), to mark or signify, at 2 Thessalonians 3:14; episemos (G1978), of note, bearing a mark.
roots_lines: Hebrew chaqaq (H2710) — to cut in, to inscribe, to decree; note it in a book for the time to come; Isaiah 30:8.
Hebrew baar (H874) — to make plain or distinct; make it plain upon tables; Habakkuk 2:2, Deuteronomy 27:8.
Greek semeioo (G4593) — to mark, to set a sign upon; note that man; 2 Thessalonians 3:14.
Greek episemos (G1978) — bearing a mark, notable, of note; used of Andronicus and Junia and of Barabbas; Romans 16:7, Matthew 27:16.
Greek noutheteo (G3560) — to admonish, to put in mind; the treatment prescribed for the noted brother; 2 Thessalonians 3:15.
usage: “Note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come” — prophecy committed to writing on purpose.
“Note that man… that he may be ashamed” — the discipline whose aim is stated in the same breath.
“Of note among the apostles” — the same word for honour.

pos: v. (to write down, to survey and record in writing; in Joshua, to map the land)
etymology: Latin describere, to write down or copy out, from de-, down, and scribere, to write. In Joshua 18 the Hebrew kathab means simply to write, and the writing is a survey.
biblical_def: The word belongs almost entirely to one scene, and it is a scene about faith. Seven tribes had not yet taken their inheritance, and Joshua rebukes their slackness, then sets them a task: “Give out from among you three men for each tribe: and I will send them, and they shall rise, and go through the land, and describe it according to the inheritance of them” (Jos 18:4). The survey is to be written in parts: “Ye shall therefore describe the land into seven parts, and bring the description hither to me, that I may cast lots for you here before the LORD our God” (Jos 18:6). And they went: “Joshua charged them that went to describe the land, saying, Go and walk through the land, and describe it, and come again to me” (Jos 18:8). Notice what order the two acts take. Men walk the ground and write it down honestly; then the lot is cast before the LORD, who disposes it. Human diligence does not compete with divine appointment here, it serves it — nobody drew a boundary to favour his tribe, because the lot was thrown after the writing. Proverbs states the principle: the lot is cast into the lap, but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to describe as to delineate or mark the form or figure of; and to represent a thing in words, by naming its properties, so that another may form a just notion of it.
webster_full: DESCRIBE, v.t. [L. describo; de and scribo, to write.] To delineate or mark the form or figure; as, to describe a circle.
2. To make or exhibit a figure by motion.
3. To show or represent to others in words; to communicate the resemblance of a thing, by naming its nature, form or properties.
Go and walk through the land, and describe it. Josh. xviii.
scriptures: Jos 18:4

Give out from among you three men for each tribe: and I will send them, and they shall rise, and go through the land, and describe it according to the inheritance of them; and they shall come again to me.
Jos 18:6
Ye shall therefore describe the land into seven parts, and bring the description hither to me, that I may cast lots for you here before the LORD our God.
Jos 18:8

And the men arose, and went away: and Joshua charged them that went to describe the land, saying, Go and walk through the land, and describe it, and come again to me, that I may here cast lots for you before the LORD in Shiloh.
Pro 16:9
A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.
corruption_summary: Joshua 18 is read as bare administration, when it is one of Scripture's plainest pictures of diligent human labour and sovereign divine appointment working in one act.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite mistakes are made with a passage like this. The first treats the surveying as mere background — the spiritual part is the lot, and the walking and writing are what men do while waiting for God to act. The second treats the lot as decorative — the real work was the survey, and the ceremony at Shiloh simply ratified it. Joshua's procedure refuses both. He sends men to walk the whole land, on foot, and to write it down in seven parts, which is hard and unglamorous work; and then he casts lots before the LORD, so that no tribe received its portion by the skill of its own surveyors. The doctrine of providence stands exactly here. God's appointment does not make diligence unnecessary; it makes diligence safe, because a man who knows the outcome is disposed by God can do his work honestly instead of steering it.

There is a further use for the honesty of the description itself. The men were charged to describe the land as it was, not as their tribe would wish it to be, and they did this before knowing which part would fall to them. That is the only condition under which a survey can be trusted, and it is a principle with wide application — a man who must divide anything is far more equitable when he does not yet know which share is his. Scripture's own practice of description follows the same rule. The histories record the sins of the patriarchs, the failures of the kings, and the quarrels of the apostles, describing the land as it is; a book that flattered its heroes would be easier to believe about nothing. Where modern retellings smooth the record, they are not improving the description, they are drawing the boundary before the lot is cast.
roots_summary: Hebrew kathab (H3789), to write, rendered describe in Joshua 18; with goral (H1486), the lot, and nachalah (H5159), the inheritance.
roots_lines: Hebrew kathab (H3789) — to write, to inscribe; the survey of the land written in seven parts; Joshua 18:4-8.
Hebrew goral (H1486) — a lot, a pebble cast; the means by which the described land was assigned; Joshua 18:6, Proverbs 16:33.
Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a possession received rather than earned; Joshua 18:4.
Hebrew halak (H1980) — to walk, to go; go and walk through the land, the labour behind the description; Joshua 18:8.
Greek graphe (G1124) — a writing, the Scripture; the same principle that a thing written may be examined afterward; 2 Timothy 3:16.
usage: “Go through the land, and describe it” — the survey before the lot.
“Bring the description hither to me” — honest work brought to the place of appointment.
“That I may cast lots for you here before the LORD” — diligence serving providence, not competing with it.

pos: v. (to make known by a sign; to indicate beforehand what a thing means or how it shall come to pass)
etymology: Latin significare, from signum, a sign, and facere, to make — to make a sign. The Greek semaino is the verb of the sign, and it governs how Revelation was given.
biblical_def: To signify is to make a thing known by a sign rather than by bare statement, and Scripture uses it for some of its weightiest transactions. Revelation opens with it: “The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John” (Rev 1:1) — which is the reader's warning that the book will speak in signs, and that the signs mean something definite. John uses the word twice of the cross: “This he said, signifying what death he should die” (Joh 12:33), because being lifted up was a sign of crucifixion before it was a fact of it. Peter uses it of the prophets, who searched “what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow” (1Pe 1:11). That single verse settles who was speaking in the Old Testament prophets and what He was speaking about. The word also does plain civil work: Festus thought it unreasonable “to send a prisoner, and not withal to signify the crimes laid against him” (Act 25:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to signify as to make known something by signs or words; to express or communicate; and secondly, to mean, to have or contain a certain sense.
webster_full: SIGNIFY, v.t. [L. significo; signum, a sign, and facio, to make.] To make known something by signs or words; to express or communicate to another any idea, thought, wish, purpose or command.
2. To mean; to have or contain a certain sense.
3. To import; to weigh; to have consequence.
He sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John. Rev. i.
scriptures: Rev 1:1
The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John:
This he said, signifying what death he should die.
Searching what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow.
For it seemeth to me unreasonable to send a prisoner, and not withal to signify the crimes laid against him.
corruption_summary: That Revelation was signified by signs is used to argue that its signs mean whatever a reader supplies, when a sign given by God has a fixed thing signified.
corruption_paragraphs: Revelation 1:1 tells the reader in advance how the book will be delivered: God gave it to Christ, Christ sent it by His angel, and the angel signified it to John. Everything about that chain is orderly, and the last verb is the one abused. Because the book speaks in signs — lamps, horns, a woman, a beast, a scroll — it is treated as though it were a field of images on which each generation may project its own alarms, and every era produces its confident identifications of the beast among its current enemies. A sign, however, is not a blank. It is a token standing for a definite thing, and Scripture ordinarily supplies the interpretation within itself: the seven candlesticks are the seven churches, the great whore is a city, the Lamb is Christ. The discipline the word imposes is to let the Bible explain its own signs and to hold with humility what it has not explained.

The second and greater use of the word is at 1 Peter 1:11, and it governs how the whole Old Testament is read. The prophets searched what the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, testifying beforehand of His sufferings and the glory to follow. Two things are asserted that modern critical reading denies outright: that the Spirit of Christ was the author speaking in the prophets, and that the subject signified was Christ's suffering and glory before either occurred. That is not a devotional flourish laid over the text; it is Peter's account of what prophecy was. Where the Old Testament is treated only as the religious literature of one nation, with Christ read in afterwards by the church, the apostle's statement has been set aside. The sign was given before the thing signified arrived, which is precisely why John could say of a sentence about being lifted up that it signified what death He should die.
roots_summary: Greek semaino (G4591), to give a sign, to indicate; from semeion (G4592), a sign; with deloo (G1213), to make plain, at 1 Peter 1:11.
roots_lines: Greek semaino (G4591) — to make known by a sign; he sent and signified it by his angel; Revelation 1:1, John 12:33.
Greek semeion (G4592) — a sign; the word John uses for the miracles that point beyond themselves; John 2:11.
Greek deloo (G1213) — to make plain, to declare; what the Spirit of Christ in the prophets did signify; 1 Peter 1:11.
Greek pneuma Christou — the Spirit of Christ; named by Peter as the one speaking in the prophets; 1 Peter 1:11.
Hebrew oth (H226) — a sign, a token; the rainbow, the sabbath, and the sign given to Ahaz; Genesis 9:13, Isaiah 7:14.
usage: “He sent and signified it by his angel” — the reader told in advance that signs are coming.
“Signifying what death he should die” — the sign before the fact.
“The Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify” — who was speaking in the prophets, and about whom.

pos: adj. and v. (inclined, minded to do a thing; also set in order, arranged by another's hand)
etymology: Latin disponere, to place apart, to arrange, from dis-, apart, and ponere, to place. The English keeps both senses: a man disposed to go, and a world disposed by God.
biblical_def: The word runs in two directions in the Authorized Version and the two together make a doctrine. Of men it means inclination: Apollos, “when he was disposed to pass into Achaia, the brethren wrote, exhorting the disciples to receive him: who, when he was come, helped them much which had believed through grace” (Act 18:27). Paul uses it of an ordinary decision about a supper: “If any of them that believe not bid you to a feast, and ye be disposed to go; whatsoever is set before you, eat, asking no question for conscience sake” (1Co 10:27) — a Christian may accept an unbeliever's invitation, and the conscience is not to be tortured over the meat. Of God the word means arrangement: Elihu asks, “Dost thou know when God disposed them, and caused the light of his cloud to shine?” (Job 37:15). Proverbs joins the two senses in one sentence about a man and a lot: the disposing is the LORD's. So Scripture allows a believer real inclination, real liberty, and real choice, and at the same time asserts that the ordering of all things belongs to God — and Acts 18 shows both at once, a man disposed to travel and a church helped much through grace by his arrival.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives to dispose as to set in order, to arrange, to distribute; and, in the passive, to be inclined or minded — the mind bent toward a thing.
webster_full: DISPOSE, v.t. [L. dispono; dis and pono, to set, place.] To set; to place or distribute; to arrange.
2. To regulate; to adjust; to set in right order.
3. To apply to a particular purpose; to give; to bestow.
DISPOSED, pp. Set in order; arranged; placed; adjusted; inclined; minded. Ye be disposed to go. 1 Cor. x.
scriptures: And when he was disposed to pass into Achaia, the brethren wrote, exhorting the disciples to receive him: who, when he was come, helped them much which had believed through grace:
If any of them that believe not bid you to a feast, and ye be disposed to go; whatsoever is set before you, eat, asking no question for conscience sake.
Dost thou know when God disposed them, and caused the light of his cloud to shine?
Pro 16:9
A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.
corruption_summary: Christian liberty is either abolished by scruple or stretched into license, while 1 Corinthians 10:27 gives a plain rule that does neither.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's instruction about the unbeliever's table is remarkably free, and both the strict and the loose have trouble with it. If ye be disposed to go — the apostle does not command attendance and does not forbid it; the inclination is left with the Christian. Whatsoever is set before you, eat, asking no question for conscience sake — the believer is not to conduct an inquiry into the provenance of the meat. That single rule cuts through an enormous amount of manufactured scruple, in which a Christian is made to examine the associations of every ordinary thing until he cannot eat a meal in peace. The context does not leave him without limits: the very next verse says that if a man tells him the meat was offered in sacrifice, he is to refrain, for the other man's conscience. Liberty is real, and it is governed by love rather than by a list.

The other half of the word supplies the deeper comfort. Elihu's question — dost thou know when God disposed them — puts the arranging of the clouds where the arranging of everything else belongs. A Christian is genuinely disposed to travel, to work, to marry, to accept an invitation; his inclinations are his own and he answers for them. And the same Scripture says the disposing is God's. Reformed doctrine has never resolved this by taking something away from either side, and Acts 18:27 is a small perfect example: Apollos was disposed to go to Achaia, brethren wrote letters, and the result is described as helping much those who had believed through grace. The man's inclination, the church's recommendation, and the sovereign grace of God appear in one sentence without any of the three being reduced.
roots_summary: Greek boulomai (G1014), to be minded or willing, rendered disposed in Acts 18:27 and 1 Corinthians 10:27; Hebrew sum (H7760), to set or place, of God's ordering in Job.
roots_lines: Greek boulomai (G1014) — to be minded, to purpose; when he was disposed to pass into Achaia; Acts 18:27, 1 Corinthians 10:27.
Greek thelo (G2309) — to will, to desire; the companion verb of inclination throughout the New Testament; Philippians 2:13.
Hebrew sum (H7760) — to put, set, appoint; used of God's ordering of the clouds and the light; Job 37:15.
Hebrew kun (H3559) — to establish, to direct; the LORD directeth the steps of the man who devised his way; Proverbs 16:9.
Greek charis (G5485) — grace; those at Corinth had believed through grace, and were then helped much; Acts 18:27.
usage: “When he was disposed to pass into Achaia” — a real inclination, and grace behind the result.
“If… ye be disposed to go… asking no question for conscience sake” — liberty with a plain rule.
“When God disposed them” — the same word, and the arranging is His.

pos: v. (to change a thing from what it was; used of vows, decrees, and the word of God)
etymology: Latin alterare, to make other, from alter, another. The Hebrew shanah means to repeat or to change; the Chaldee of Ezra is the same root, used of tampering with a royal decree.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses alter almost exclusively for tampering with something that has been fixed, and the tone is always prohibitive. Of a devoted beast the law says, “He shall not alter it, nor change it, a good for a bad, or a bad for a good: and if he shall at all change beast for beast, then it and the exchange thereof shall be holy” (Lev 27:10) — a vow once made is not to be renegotiated, even upward. Darius protects the rebuilding of the temple with a decree against alteration and a penalty attached: “that shall put to their hand to alter and to destroy this house of God which is at Jerusalem” (Ezr 6:12). The Medo-Persian law was famous for it, and Daniel's enemies used the fact against him: the writing was signed “that it be not changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” (Dan 6:8). Then the word is lifted to its highest use, where God speaks of Himself: “My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips” (Psa 89:34). Human decrees are unalterable by a legal fiction; God's word is unalterable by His nature.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to alter as to make some change in; to make different in some particular; to vary in some degree, without an entire change.
webster_full: ALTER, v.t. [L. alter, another.] To make some change in; to make different in some particular; to vary in some degree, without an entire change.
2. To change entirely or materially; as, to alter an opinion.
ALTER, v.i. To vary; to change; to become different.
My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips. Ps. lxxxix.
scriptures: He shall not alter it, nor change it, a good for a bad, or a bad for a good: and if he shall at all change beast for beast, then it and the exchange thereof shall be holy.
My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips.
Dan 6:8
Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it be not changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not.
Mal 3:6
For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.
corruption_summary: The living church is now expected to alter the deposit it received in order to keep it credible, though Scripture attaches a curse to adding and diminishing and grounds our safety in a God who does not change.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy forbids adding to the word or diminishing ought from it, and Revelation closes the canon with the same double prohibition and a penalty. Both halves matter, because alteration usually presents itself as one or the other and rarely as both at once. Addition arrives as enrichment: a tradition, a practice, a further revelation, offered as completing what Scripture left bare. Diminishing arrives as candour: a doctrine quietly retired because it has become costly to hold — substitutionary punishment, eternal judgment, the created order of man and woman, the exclusiveness of Christ. Neither is a small correction of detail. The Authorized Version's use of the word is instructive here, because Leviticus 27:10 forbids exchanging the devoted beast a good for a bad, or a bad for a good. Even an improvement is forbidden. What has been given to God is not the giver's to revise.

Behind the prohibition stands the doctrine that makes the Christian faith stable at all. God says, I am the LORD, I change not, and the consequence He draws from it is not abstract but pastoral: therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed. His immutability is the reason a covenant people survive their own inconstancy. Psalm 89 is the great instance, because the psalm is written in the middle of a disaster, its writer complaining that the crown has been cast to the ground, and it still records God saying He will not alter the thing gone out of His lips. That is the ground of assurance. If God could revise His word as men revise theirs, no promise could be leaned on for a decade, let alone an eternity; and Hebrews sets the same immutability in the Son — Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
roots_summary: Hebrew shanah (H8138), to change or repeat; Chaldee shena (H8133), to alter, used of decrees in Ezra and Daniel; set against the divine lo shanithi, I change not, of Malachi 3:6.
roots_lines: Hebrew shanah (H8138) — to change, to alter; he shall not alter it, nor change it; Leviticus 27:10.
Chaldee shena (H8133) — to alter or be changed; the decrees of Darius and of the Medes and Persians; Ezra 6:12, Daniel 6:8.
Hebrew shanah in Malachi 3:6 — I am the LORD, I change not; the immutability from which the mercy is drawn.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; the thing God will not break nor alter; Psalm 89:34.
Greek aparabatos (G531) — unchangeable, not passing to another; used of Christ's unalterable priesthood; Hebrews 7:24.
usage: “He shall not alter it, nor change it, a good for a bad, or a bad for a good” — even an improvement forbidden.
“Nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips” — said in the middle of a disaster.
“I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed” — the doctrine and its comfort in one verse.
